course_title: Lithic Analysis: Current and Future Directions for Research and Heritage Management
course_description:
This course offers instruction in the theoretical, archaeological and experimental basis of stone artefact analysis in an Australian and global context. The course covers lithic technology in human evolution, reconstructing past settlement and subsistence practices, typology and classification, lithic assemblage analysis, as well as applications in heritage management. Students will become familiar with identifying fracture mechanics and fracture features, flintknapping and replication, recording and analysing stone artefacts, experimental research design, lithic illustration, conjoining, and familiarity with new directions in lithic analysis.

This course trains students in stone artefact identification and the principles of contemporary lithic analysis. It will cover applications in both research and heritage. The course takes a two-hour lecture and two-hour laboratory format in order to provide opportunity to examine, observe, identify and analyse stone artefacts. Lectures will cover the core theoretical and methodological aspects of lithic analysis with reference to key case studies and examples. The course covers fracture mechanics, raw materials, fracture feature identification, classification theory and practice, major periods and changes in lithic technology throughout human evolution, refitting, illustration, attribute and debitage analysis, use-wear analysis, heritage applications as well as new directions in lithic analysis. Students will have the opportunity to learn the fundamentals of replicative flintknapping with hands-on tuition face to face. Lectures and practicals will be face-to-face, with some online practical content. Attendance of the face to face classes is mandatory.

learning_outcomes.description: Understand and discuss key ideas about lithics - Understand and critique core disciplinary literature, and make connections between theory and practice.

Identify stone artefacts - You will be able to identify a range of complete and broken flaked and ground stone artefacts. You will be able to identify common raw material and stone tool types found in Australia and elsewhere. You will be able to name fracture features and list the types of features commonly found on different kinds of artefacts.

Carry out basic lithic analysis - You will be able to understand and evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches to lithic analysis in Australia and abroad. You will be armed with the basic skills of artefact recording, summarising, comparing and reporting, including some basic statistical anlaysis.
Construct a research design for specific analyses - You will be able to design detailed lithic analyses for different kinds of research questions and for heritage applications.

Illustrate stone tools - You will be able to determine the appropriate kinds of artefacts to illustrate for different purposes as well as the appropriate style of illustration for different artefact types.
Understand heritage applications for lithics - Understand the requirements of different kinds of heritage work, from survey to specialist analysis to curation and presentation of finds.

assessment_details.title: Lithic Analysis Report
assessment_details.task_description: Students will each be given an ‘assemblage’ of stone tools with contextual information about the ‘site’ these artefacts came from. The assemblage is broken into four levels with a different technology and composition of raw materials in each. The study will employ classification and attribute analysis to identify reduction techniques, describe and compare artefacts from each level and will provide interpretive statements about technological change and behaviour at the site (such as organisation of technology, changes in provisioning, changes in raw material rationing, etc). Key artefact types must be photographed and/or illustrated. The report will also employ some common indices of fragmentation, identifiability and richness for each level to assess the information potential and significance of the site. The goals of the assignment are to enable students to write a research design, perform a manageable lithic analysis, make choices about appropriate variables, take appropriate measurements, compile and present data, and develop conclusions about the materials while reflecting on the research goals. Generation of summary tables and basic statistics will be necessary. These analytical procedures will be demonstrated and taught in class before the assignment is due. Marking criteria: Criteria including rubrics are available in the ‘Assessments’ folder on the course Blackboard site. AI Use: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which AI may provide limited support and guidance. A failure to reference AI use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct Policy. Students may be required to complete an AI usage declaration and submit it with their assessment. Additional resources are available through UQ AI Student Hub . learning_activities.topic: 1. Introduction to lithics and fracture mechanics An introduction to stone artefacts, the types of rocks typically used to make stone artefacts and an in-depth look into how stone fractures during knapping. Learning outcomes: L01, L02
Practical 1 1. Hard hammer and bipolar flaking, fracture features 2. Raw Materials Learning outcomes: L02
2. Describing Lithics: Typology & Technology Major directions lithic analysts have taken towards describing stone tool technologies. Learning outcomes: L01, L03
Practical 2 1. Attribute identification 2. Fragmentation, cores and flakes sorting Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
3. Principles of classification (Online) Lithic classification schemes, their utility, and common issues with their application. Learning outcomes: L01, L03
Practical 3 1. Database use, flake and core measurements 2. Single-platform & multi-platform cores Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
4. Attribute, debitage and refit analysis (Online) Developing practical skills of identifying lithic attribute features. Learning outcomes: L01, L03
Practical 4 1. Refitting and lithic illustration 2. In-class revision for exam Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L05
5. New Directions for Lithic Analysis Computer-based approaches to the study of stone tools.
In-Class Exam In-class laboratory exam for weeks 1-4. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

6. Lower Palaeolithic & Early Stone Age Beginning an overview of the archaeological record by looking at the earliest stone tool industries such as the Lomekwian, Oldowan, and Acheulean. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Practical 5 1. Choppers, handaxes, cleavers and bifacial knapping 2. Assemblage interpretation Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

7. The Middle Palaeolithic & Middle Stone Age The origins of modern humans in the African Middle Stone Age. Neanderthal, modern human and Denisovan Middle Palaeolithic technologies. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Practical 6 Levallois flaking and potato knapping Scraper types and retouch measurement Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04
8. Australian and New Guinean lithics A close look at Australian stone artefacts. Learning outcomes: L01, L02
Practical 7 Examining Australian and New Guinean lithic material Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

9. Upper Palaeolithic & Later Stone Age/Neolithic The Late Stone Age record in Africa reflects human population increase and diversification, while the Upper Palaeolithic tracks the spread of modern humans into Europe and Asia, with new adaptations to these cold environments. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Practical 8 Blade technology and potato blade cores In-class review for exam Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Mid-Semester Break No Class
Public Holiday

11. Introduction to Use-wear Analysis (Online) "What were stone tools used for?" One of the ways archaeologists attempt to answer this basic question about the past. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05, L06
In-Class Exam In-class laboratory exam for weeks 1-9 Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

12. Lithics in Heritage Management Cultural heritage management practices, recording lithics and sites, assessing cultural and archaeological significance, predictive modelling and report writing. Learning outcomes: L06
Practical 9 Using stone tools at ATARC and producing use-wear Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

13. Interpreting Lithics and Overview of Course Looking at how lithics have been used to interpret how people lived in the past. An overview of the course will also be presented. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L06
Practical 10 Metric analysis and data handling for lithics report Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L06
